questions.q: You are making a treatment decision with a 72-year-old man with colon cancer. You are aware of several good studies that have shown that a certain drug combination prolongs the life of patients with colon cancer. However, all the patients in these studies were much younger. Which of the statements below is correct?
opts: Given these studies, the decision about this treatment is a matter of personal judgment.

Correct. Generalizing from younger to older patients is a matter of personal judgment based on whatever facts there are that bear on whether older patients respond to treatment the same as younger patients. Internal validity is about whether the results are correct for the patients in the study, not about whether they are correct for other kinds of patients. Both bias and chance affect internal validity.

questions.q: A study was done to determine whether regular exercise lowers the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). An exercise program was offered to employees of a factory, and the rates of subsequent coronary events were compared in employees who volunteered for the program and those who did not volunteer. The development of CHD was determined by means of regular voluntary checkups, including a careful history, an electrocardiogram, and a review of routine health records. Surprisingly, the members of the exercise group developed higher rates of CHD even though fewer of them smoked cigarettes. This result is least likely to be explained by which of the following?
opts: The volunteers did not actually increase their exercise and the amount of exercise was the same in the two groups.

Correct. If volunteers had the same amount of exercise as the nonvolunteers, a difference in the rate of CHD could not be explained by this variable. Differences in the groups (selection bias) or in the methods used to determine CHD (measurement bias) could account for the finding.
The volunteers were at higher risk for developing CHD than those not volunteering before the study began.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The volunteers did not actually increase their exercise and the amount of exercise was the same in the two groups. See the explanation under it.
Volunteers got more checkups, and silent myocardial infarctions were, therefore, more likely to have been diagnosed in the exercise group.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The volunteers did not actually increase their exercise and the amount of exercise was the same in the two groups. See the explanation under it.

questions.q:
Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is a serious condition that occasionally can lead to pulmonary embolism and death. The incidence of DVT is increased by several genetic and environmental factors, including oral contraceptives (OCs) and a genetic mutation, factor V Leiden. These two risk factors, OCs and factor V Leiden, interact. Heterozygotes for factor V Leiden have 4 to 10 times the risk of DVT of the general population. In women without the genetic mutation, incidence of DVT rises from about 0.8/10,000 women/yr among those not on OCs to 3.0/10,000 women/yr for those taking the pill. The baseline incidence of DVT in heterozygotes for factor V Leiden is 5.7/10,000 women/yr, rising to 28.5/10,000 women/yr among those taking OCs. Mutations for factor V Leiden occur in about 5% of whites but are absent in Africans and Asians.

Not the best answer. The best answer is: One of the baseline variables is strongly related to prognosis. See the explanation under it.
One of the baseline variables is strongly related to prognosis.

Correct. Stratified randomization is one approach to control of confounding, especially useful when a characteristic is strongly related to outcome—and also when the study is small enough that one worries that randomization might not create groups with similar prognosis.
Assignment to treatment group is not blinded.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: One of the baseline variables is strongly related to prognosis. See the explanation under it.
Many patients are expected to drop out.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: One of the baseline variables is strongly related to prognosis. See the explanation under it.
An intention-to-treat analysis is planned.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: One of the baseline variables is strongly related to prognosis. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial is analyzed according to the treatment each patient actually received. Which of the following best describes this approach to analysis?
opts: Superiority
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Per-protocol. See the explanation under it.
Intention-to-treat
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Per-protocol. See the explanation under it.
Noninferiority
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Per-protocol. See the explanation under it.
Open label
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Per-protocol. See the explanation under it.
Per-protocol
Correct. In per-protocol analyses, outcomes are attributed to the treatment patients actually receive, not the treatment group they were randomized to, which is an intention-to-treat analysis.

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial, a beta-blocking drug is found to be more effective than placebo for stage fright. Patients taking the beta-blocker tended to have a lower pulse rate and to feel more lethargic, which are known effects of this drug. For which of the following is blinding possible?
opts: The patients' physicians
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The investigators who assigned patients to treatment groups. See the explanation under it.
The investigators who assigned patients to treatment groups

Correct. Side effects of the drug, both symptoms and signs, would alert patients and doctors to who is taking the active drug but could not affect random allocation, which was done before the drug was begun.
The patients in the trial
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The investigators who assigned patients to treatment groups. See the explanation under it.
The investigators who assess outcome
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The investigators who assigned patients to treatment groups. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes “equipoise” as the rationale for a randomized trial of two drugs?
opts: The drugs are known to be equally effective.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Neither drug is known to be more effective than the other. See the explanation under it.
One of the drugs is known to be more toxic.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Neither drug is known to be more effective than the other. See the explanation under it.
Neither drug is known to be more effective than the other.

Correct. For a randomized controlled trial to be ethical, there should not be conclusive evidence that one of the experimental treatments is better or worse than the other—that is, the scientific community should be in a state of “equipoise” on that issue. There may be opinions as to which is better, but no consensus. There may be some evidence bearing on the comparison, but the evidence should not be conclusive.
Although one drug is more effective, the other drug is easier to take with fewer side effects.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Neither drug is known to be more effective than the other. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Antibiotic A is the established treatment for community-acquired pneumonia, but it is expensive and has many side effects. A new drug, antibiotic B, has just been developed for community-acquired pneumonia and is less expensive and has fewer side effects, but its efficacy, relative to drug A, is not well established. Which of the following would be the best kind of trial for evaluating drug B?
opts: Superiority
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Noninferiority. See the explanation under it.
Crossover
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Noninferiority. See the explanation under it.
Cluster
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Noninferiority. See the explanation under it.
Noninferiority

Correct. Because the new drug has advantages over the old one, but comparative effectiveness is unknown, the appropriate randomized trial comparing the two would be a noninferiority trial to establish whether the new drug is no less efficacious.
Equivalence
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Noninferiority. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial of two drugs for coronary artery disease, the primary outcome is a composite of acute myocardial infarction, severe angina pectoris, and cardiac death. Which of the following is the main advantage of this approach?
opts: There are more outcomes events than there would be for any of the individual outcomes.

Correct. Making the primary outcome of a trial a composite of clinically important and related outcomes increases the number of outcome events and, therefore, the ability of the trial to detect an effect if it is present. The disadvantage is that the intervention may affect the component outcomes differently, and reliance on the composite outcome alone might mask this effect.
All outcomes are equally affected by the interventions.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There are more outcomes events than there would be for any of the individual outcomes. See the explanation under it.
The trial has more generalizability.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There are more outcomes events than there would be for any of the individual outcomes. See the explanation under it.
Each of the individual outcomes is important in its own right.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There are more outcomes events than there would be for any of the individual outcomes. See the explanation under it.
If one outcome is infrequent, others make up for it.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There are more outcomes events than there would be for any of the individual outcomes. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: In a randomized controlled trial comparing two approaches to managing children with bronchiolitis, baseline characteristics of the 200 children in the trial are somewhat different in the two randomly allocated groups. Which of the following might explain this finding?
opts: “Bad luck” in randomization
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Both. See the explanation under it.
A breakdown in allocation concealment
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Both. See the explanation under it.
Both

Correct. bad luck in randomization and breakdown in allocation concealment (by bad methods or cheating) would show up as differences in baseline characteristics of patients in a trial. Small differences are expected and the challenge is to decide how large the differences must be for them to raise concern.
Neither
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Both. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is usually learned from a Phase III drug trial?
opts: The relationship between dose and efficacy
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Efficacy or effectiveness. See the explanation under it.
Rates of uncommon side effects
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Efficacy or effectiveness. See the explanation under it.
Efficacy or effectiveness

Correct. The usual drug trials reported in the clinical literature are “Phase III” trials, intended to establish efficacy or effectiveness. Further study, with postmarketing surveillance, is needed to detect uncommon side effects. Responses A and D are about what Phase I and Phase II trials are meant to establish.
The dose range that is well tolerated
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Efficacy or effectiveness. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is the main advantage of randomized controlled trials over observational studies of treatment effects?
opts: Fewer ethical challenges
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Prevention of confounding. See the explanation under it.
Prevention of confounding

Correct. is the main advantage of randomized controlled trials, which is why they are valued despite being ethically complicated, slower, and more expensive. Whether they resemble usual care depends on how the trial is designed.
Resemble usual care
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Prevention of confounding. See the explanation under it.
Quicker answer
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Prevention of confounding. See the explanation under it.
Less expensive
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Prevention of confounding. See the explanation under it.

questions.q:
A study was conducted to determine whether a fecal occult blood screening test reduced mortality from colorectal cancer. People of ages 50 to 60 years were randomized to the screening test or to a control group and followed for 13 years. Over this time, there were 323 cancer cases and 82 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,570 people randomized to annual screening; there were 356 cancers and 121 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,394 people randomized to the control group. Investigators found that for dried stool cards the sensitivity was 80% and the specificity 98%. If the cards were rehydrated, sensitivity improved to 90% and specificity decreased to 90%.

What is the relative risk reduction of colorectal mortality in the screened group?
opts: Correct. The relative risk reduction of colorectal cancer mortality is the absolute risk reduction divided by the cancer mortality rate in the control group . The colorectal cancer mortality rate in the screened group = 82/15,570 = 0.0053 The colorectal cancer mortality rate in the control group = 121/15,394 = 0.0079 Absolute risk reduction = 0.0079 – 0.0053 = 0.0026 Relative risk reduction of colorectal cancer mortality due to screening = 0.0026/0.0079 = 0.33 or 33% reduction. An alternative approach calculates the complement of relative risk. In the example, the relative risk of colorectal mortality in the screened compared to the control group was 0.0053/0.0079 = 0.67. The complement of 0.67 = 1.00 – 0.67 = 0.33 or 33%.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 33%. See the explanation under it.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 33%. See the explanation under it.

questions.q:
A study was conducted to determine whether a fecal occult blood screening test reduced mortality from colorectal cancer. People of ages 50 to 60 years were randomized to the screening test or to a control group and followed for 13 years. Over this time, there were 323 cancer cases and 82 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,570 people randomized to annual screening; there were 356 cancers and 121 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,394 people randomized to the control group. Investigators found that for dried stool cards the sensitivity was 80% and the specificity 98%. If the cards were rehydrated, sensitivity improved to 90% and specificity decreased to 90%.

How many patients would you need to screen over the next 13 years to prevent one death from colorectal cancer?
opts: Not the best answer. The best answer is: 385. See the explanation under it.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 385. See the explanation under it.
Correct. The number needed to screen is the reciprocal of absolute risk reduction, 1/0.0026, or 385.

questions.q:
A study was conducted to determine whether a fecal occult blood screening test reduced mortality from colorectal cancer. People of ages 50 to 60 years were randomized to the screening test or to a control group and followed for 13 years. Over this time, there were 323 cancer cases and 82 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,570 people randomized to annual screening; there were 356 cancers and 121 colorectal cancer deaths in the 15,394 people randomized to the control group. Investigators found that for dried stool cards the sensitivity was 80% and the specificity 98%. If the cards were rehydrated, sensitivity improved to 90% and specificity decreased to 90%.

If rehydrated instead of dried stool cards were used:
opts: Screened patients would need fewer colonoscopies.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The probability of disease with a negative test would decrease. See the explanation under it.
The positive predictive value would increase.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The probability of disease with a negative test would decrease. See the explanation under it.
The probability of disease with a negative test would decrease.

Correct. Rehydrated cards have a higher sensitivity and lower specificity. To assess the overall effect of these changes on predictive value, one approach is to calculate likelihood ratios. The positive likelihood of dried cards would be sensitivity/(1 - specificity) = 0.80/(1 - 0.98) = 40. With rehydration, it would be 0.9/(1 - 0.9) = 9. The negative likelihood ratio would be (1 - sensitivity)/specificity = (1 - 0.8)/0.98 = 0.20 for dried cards, and (1 - 0.9)/0.9 = 0.11 with rehydration. Thus for a given prevalence of cancer, rehydration would lead to a lower positive predictive value (with more false positives and colonoscopies), a lower negative predictive value.

questions.q:
In a randomized controlled trial of screening chest x-rays and sputum cytology for lung cancer, approximately 9,000 men were randomized to screening for 6 years or a control group. After 20 years, the lung cancer mortality was the same in both groups (4.4/1,000 person-years in the screened group and 3.9/1,000 person-years in the control group). However, the median survival for patients diagnosed with lung cancer was 1.3 years in the screened group and 0.9 years in the control group. Also, screening found more lung cancer—206 cancers were diagnosed in the screened group and 160 in the control group.

What is the best conclusion after reading such a study?
opts: Finding a better survival rate but not a change in the mortality rate of lung cancer makes no sense and the study must be flawed.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Because mortality did not change, screening may have resulted in more “disease time” for those diagnosed with lung cancer. See the explanation under it.
Because mortality did not change, screening may have resulted in more “disease time” for those diagnosed with lung cancer.

Correct. Lead time (the period time between the detection of a disease on screening and when it would ordinarily be diagnosed because the patient seeks medical care due to symptoms) can be associated with what appears to be an improvement in survival. The fact that mortality did not improve after screening in this randomized trial raises the possibility that lead-time bias is responsible for the result. Another possible cause of the finding is overdiagnosis.
Improved survival demonstrates screening was effective in the study.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Because mortality did not change, screening may have resulted in more “disease time” for those diagnosed with lung cancer. See the explanation under it.

questions.q:
In a randomized controlled trial of screening chest x-rays and sputum cytology for lung cancer, approximately 9,000 men were randomized to screening for 6 years or a control group. After 20 years, the lung cancer mortality was the same in both groups (4.4/1,000 person-years in the screened group and 3.9/1,000 person-years in the control group). However, the median survival for patients diagnosed with lung cancer was 1.3 years in the screened group and 0.9 years in the control group. Also, screening found more lung cancer—206 cancers were diagnosed in the screened group and 160 in the control group.

What bias is the best explanation for the improved survival in the face of no improvement in the mortality rate in this study?
opts: Lead-time bias
Correct. See answer for 10.4.
Survival bias
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Lead-time bias. See the explanation under it.
Compliance bias
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Lead-time bias. See the explanation under it.
Length-time bias
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Lead-time bias. See the explanation under it.

questions.q:
In a randomized controlled trial of screening chest x-rays and sputum cytology for lung cancer, approximately 9,000 men were randomized to screening for 6 years or a control group. After 20 years, the lung cancer mortality was the same in both groups (4.4/1,000 person-years in the screened group and 3.9/1,000 person-years in the control group). However, the median survival for patients diagnosed with lung cancer was 1.3 years in the screened group and 0.9 years in the control group. Also, screening found more lung cancer—206 cancers were diagnosed in the screened group and 160 in the control group.

What is the most likely reason for the fact that 206 lung cancers were found in the screened group and only 160 in the control group?
opts: There were more smokers in the screened group.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Screening picked up some cancers that would not have come to medical attention without screening. See the explanation under it.
Screening found cancers earlier and the number of cancers in the control group will catch up over time.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Screening picked up some cancers that would not have come to medical attention without screening. See the explanation under it.
Screening picked up some cancers that would not have come to medical attention without screening.

Correct. Overdiagnosis, the detection of lesions that would not have caused clinical symptoms or morbidity, is likely because, even after 20 years, the number of cancers in the control group remained fewer than that in the screened group. Increased numbers of cancers in the screened group could occur if there were more smokers in the screened group, but randomization should have made that possibility unlikely.

questions.q: Researchers in Denmark looked at the incidence of breast cancer over 3 decades in areas of the country where mammogram screening was introduced compared to locations where screening was not offered. Small invasive cancers (<2 cm) were found more frequently in the screened group, but the incidence of large invasive cancers (>2 cm) was similar for the screened and unscreened groups. These findings remained after controlling for age differences. Which of the following is true?
opts: If lead-time bias is present, both cancer survival rates and cancer mortality rates will be lower in the screening group.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Many of the smaller tumors detected may not have become clinically significant. See the explanation under it.
Many of the smaller tumors detected may not have become clinically significant

Correct. The findings could be due to overdiagnosis, where the smaller tumors detected would not have become clinically significant. With lead-time bias, cancers are diagnosed earlier (thus increasing the apparent survival with cancer), even if cancer mortality rates are unchanged.
Overdiagnosis is not present because the cancers found were invasive.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Many of the smaller tumors detected may not have become clinically significant. See the explanation under it.
The study does not account for possible changes in the cancer incidence over time.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Many of the smaller tumors detected may not have become clinically significant. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: A review compared the performance of HPV testing versus cytology (pap smears) for cervical cancer screening. Compared to cytology, HPV testing had better detection of precancerous lesions that would be treated to prevent subsequent cancers. However, it also had a higher false-positive rate. Which of the following is incorrect?
opts: HPV is more sensitive than cytology for screening.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The positive predictive value is higher for HPV than cytology. See the explanation under it.
HPV is less specific than cytology for screening.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The positive predictive value is higher for HPV than cytology. See the explanation under it.
More frequent testing may improve the sensitivity of cytology.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The positive predictive value is higher for HPV than cytology. See the explanation under it.
The positive predictive value is higher for HPV than cytology.

Correct. Compared to cytology, a single HPV test is more sensitive (it detects a higher percentage of lesions) but less specific (for patients without lesions, there are fewer true negatives and more false positives). HPV testing compared to cytology therefore has a better negative predictive value but lower positive predictive value for a given prevalence. Sensitivity of either test can be improved and specificity worsened with more frequent testing.

questions.q: When assessing a new vaccine, which of the following is least important:
opts: Efficacy in preventing the disease
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cost of giving the vaccine. See the explanation under it.
Safety of the vaccine
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cost of giving the vaccine. See the explanation under it.
Danger of the disease
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cost of giving the vaccine. See the explanation under it.
Cost of giving the vaccine

Correct. Several important questions are to be considered when assessing a new vaccine, including: (i) Has the vaccine been shown to be efficacious (did it work under ideal circumstances when everyone in the intervention group received the vaccine and no one in a comparable control group did) and was it effective (under everyday circumstances, which people in the intervention group did not receive the vaccine)? (ii) Is the vaccine safe? (iii) Is the burden of suffering of the condition the vaccine protects against important enough to consider a preventive measure?, and (iv) Is it cost-effective? Cost of the vaccine is only one component of an analysis of cost-effectiveness.

questions.q: When the same test is used in diagnostic and screening situations, which of the following statements is most likely correct?
opts: The sensitivity and specificity will likely be the same in both situations.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Disease prevalence will be higher in the diagnostic situation. See the explanation under it.
The positive predictive value will be higher in a screening situation.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Disease prevalence will be higher in the diagnostic situation. See the explanation under it.
Overdiagnosis is equally likely in both situations.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Disease prevalence will be higher in the diagnostic situation. See the explanation under it.
Disease prevalence will be higher in the diagnostic situation.

Correct. Disease prevalence is lower in presumably well people (screening) than in symptomatic patients (diagnosis). As a result, positive predictive value will be lower in screening. Because screening is aimed at picking up early disease, the sensitivity of most tests is lower in screening than in patients with more advanced disease. Overdiagnosis is less likely in diagnostic situations when symptomatic patients have more late-stage disease.

questions.q: A study found that volunteers for a new screening test had better health outcomes than people who refused testing. Which of the following statements most likely explains the finding?
opts: Volunteers tend to be more interested in their health than those who do not participate in preventive activities.

Correct. Volunteers for preventive care are more compliant with advice about medical care and usually have better health outcomes than those who reject preventive care. This effect is so strong that it is seen even when volunteers are taking placebo medications.
People who refuse screening are usually healthier than those who accept.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Volunteers tend to be more interested in their health than those who do not participate in preventive activities. See the explanation under it.
Volunteers for screening are more likely to need screening than those who refuse.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Volunteers tend to be more interested in their health than those who do not participate in preventive activities. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: All of the following statements are correct except:
opts: The gold standard for a test used for diagnosis may be different than that for the same test when used for screening.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The incidence method cannot be used to calculate sensitivity for cancer screening tests. See the explanation under it.
The incidence method cannot be used to calculate sensitivity for cancer screening tests.

Correct. The incidence method is particularly useful when calculating sensitivity for screening tests because it takes into account the possibility of overdiagnosis. The gold standard for screening tests almost always involves a follow-up interval. The first round of screening picks up prevalent as well as incident cases, inflating the number compared to later screening rounds.
When a screening program is begun, more people with disease are found on the first round of screening than on later rounds.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The incidence method cannot be used to calculate sensitivity for cancer screening tests. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: For a cost-effectiveness analysis of a preventive activity, which kinds of costs should be included?
opts: Medical costs, such as those associated with delivering the preventive intervention
Not the best answer. The best answer is: All of the above. See the explanation under it.
All medical costs, including diagnostic follow-up of positive tests and treatment for persons diagnosed with disease, with and without the preventive activity
Not the best answer. The best answer is: All of the above. See the explanation under it.
Indirect costs, such as loss of income due to time off from work, among patients receiving the prevention and those who develop the disease
Not the best answer. The best answer is: All of the above. See the explanation under it.
Indirect costs for both patients and care givers
Not the best answer. The best answer is: All of the above. See the explanation under it.
All of the above

Correct. Cost-effectiveness should be estimated in a way that captures all costs of the preventive activity and all the costs associated with diagnosis and treatment, wherever they occur, to determine the costs of the preventive activity from a societal perspective. All costs that occur when prevention is not done are subtracted from all costs when prevention is done to estimate the cost for a given health effect.

questions.q: A randomized controlled trial of thrombolytic therapy versus angioplasty for acute myocardial infarction finds no difference in the main outcome, survival to discharge from hospital. The investigators explored whether this was also true for subgroups of patients defined by age, number of vessels affected, ejection fraction, comorbidity, and other patient characteristics. Which of the following is not true about this subgroup analysis?
opts: Examining subgroups increases the chance of a false-positive (misleading statistically significant) result in one of the comparisons.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are bad scientific practice and should not be done. See the explanation under it.
Examining subgroups increases the chance of a false-negative finding in one of these subgroups, relative to the main result.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are bad scientific practice and should not be done. See the explanation under it.
Subgroup analyses are bad scientific practice and should not be done.
Correct. Although subgroup analyses risk false-positive and false-negative conclusions, they provide information that can help clinicians as long as their limitations are kept in mind.
Reporting results in subgroups helps clinicians tailor information in the study to individual patients.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are bad scientific practice and should not be done. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: A new drug for hyperlipidemia was compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial of 10,000 patients. After 2 years, serum cholesterol (the primary outcome) was 238 mg/dL in the group receiving the new drug and 240 mg/dL in the group receiving the old drug (P <0.001). Which of the following best describes the meaning of the P value in this study?
opts: Bias is unlikely to account for the observed difference.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000. See the explanation under it.
The difference is clinically important.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000. See the explanation under it.
A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000.
Correct. The P value describes the risk of a false-positive conclusion and has nothing directly to do with bias and statistical power or the generalizability or clinical importance of the finding.
The results are generalizable to other patients with hypertension.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000. See the explanation under it.
The statistical power of this study was inadequate.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A difference as big as or bigger than what was observed could have arisen by chance less than one time in 1,000. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: In a well-designed clinical trial of treatment for ovarian cancer, remission rate at 1 year is 30% in patients offered a new drug and 20% in those offered a placebo. The P value is 0.4. Which of the following best describes the interpretation of this result?
opts: Both treatments are effective.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other. See the explanation under it.
Neither treatment is effective.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other. See the explanation under it.
The statistical power of this study is 60%.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other. See the explanation under it.
The best estimate of treatment effect size is 0.4.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other. See the explanation under it.
There is insufficient information to decide whether one treatment is better than the other.

Correct. The P value is not small enough to establish that a treatment effect exists and provides no information on whether a clinically important effect could have been missed because of inadequate statistical power.

questions.q: In a cohort study, vitamin A intake was found to be a risk factor for hip fracture in women. The relative risk (highest quintile vs. lowest quintile) was 1.48, and the 95% confidence interval was 1.05–2.07. Which of the following best describes the meaning of this confidence interval?
opts: The association is not statistically significant at the P <0.05 level.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk. See the explanation under it.
A strong association between vitamin A intake and hip fracture was established.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk. See the explanation under it.
The statistical power of this study is 95%.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk. See the explanation under it.
There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk.

Correct. The result was statistically significant, if one wanted to think of the role of chance in that way, because it excluded a relative risk of 1.0. Response D described the information the confidence interval contributes.
Bias is an unlikely explanation for this result.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There is a 95% chance that a range of relative risks as low as 1.05 and as high as 2.07 includes the true risk. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best reason for calling P ≤0.05 “statistically significant?”
opts: It definitively rules out a false-positive conclusion.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb. See the explanation under it.
It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb.
Correct. Calling P ≤0.05 “statistically significant” is a useful convention but otherwise has no particular mathematical or clinical meaning.
It rules out a type II error.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb. See the explanation under it.
It is a way of establishing a clinically important effect size.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb. See the explanation under it.
Larger or smaller P values do not provide useful information.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It is an arbitrarily chosen but useful rule of thumb. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is the biggest advantage of multivariable modeling?
opts: Models can control for many variables simultaneously.

Correct. Models do depend on assumptions about the data, are not done in a standard way, and are meant to complement stratified analyses, not replace them. Although they might be used in large randomized trials, they are not particularly useful in that situation because randomization of a large number of patients has already made confounding very unlikely.
Models do not depend on assumptions about the data.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Models can control for many variables simultaneously. See the explanation under it.
There is a standardized and reproducible approach to modeling.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Models can control for many variables simultaneously. See the explanation under it.
Models make stratified analyses unnecessary.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Models can control for many variables simultaneously. See the explanation under it.
Models can control for confounding in large randomized controlled trials.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Models can control for many variables simultaneously. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: A trial randomizes 30,000 patients to two treatment groups of similar size: one offered chemoprevention and the other usual care. How frequently must a side effect of chemoprevention occur for the study to have a good chance of observing at least one such side effect?

Applying the rule of thumb mentioned in this chapter (but solving for event rate, not sample size), 15,000 divided by 3 or a 1/5,000 event rate could be detected with 15,000 people under observation.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 1/5,000. See the explanation under it.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 1/5,000. See the explanation under it.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 1/5,000. See the explanation under it.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: 1/5,000. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: A noninferiority randomized trial compared arthroscopic surgery versus physical therapy for knee injury with meniscal tears. The primary outcome was improvement in knee function, using a scale of 0 to 100, with better function indicated by higher scores. The noninferiority margin was defined as an 8-point difference in improvement, and a one-sided α level was set at 0.025. At 2 years follow-up, the knee surgery group had an improvement in function of 3.6 greater than the physical therapy group, P = 0.001 for noninferiority. Based on the results, which conclusion is true?
opts: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy.

Correct. The null hypothesis for this noninferiority trial is that the alternative treatment, physical therapy, is worse than the established treatment, surgery. The margin selected by the investigators is a judgment of what level of difference in function between the two groups would be clinically important. Although surgery had higher improvement in knee function scores than physical therapy, the difference between the two, 3.6, was below the margin of 8.0. In addition, significance testing showed that it would be unlikely that the true difference would be 8 or more. Thus the null hypothesis is rejected, and the conclusion from the study is that no clinically important difference exists between the two treatments, that is, physical therapy is noninferior to surgery.
There was a statistically significant greater improvement in knee function for the surgery group compared to the physical therapy group.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy. See the explanation under it.
The study could not reject the null hypothesis based on these findings.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy. See the explanation under it.
The study may have erroneously concluded a true difference exists between surgery and physical therapy.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy. See the explanation under it.
A smaller margin would have been more likely to be statistically significant.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: There was no clinically important difference between surgery and physical therapy. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is least related to the statistical power of a study with a dichotomous outcome?
opts: Effect size
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The statistical test used. See the explanation under it.
Type I error
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The statistical test used. See the explanation under it.
Rate of outcome events in the control group
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The statistical test used. See the explanation under it.
Type II error
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The statistical test used. See the explanation under it.
The statistical test used

Correct. Statistical power depends on the joint effects of all of the factors mentioned in A–D. It may vary a bit with the statistical test used to calculate it, but this is not the main determinate of sample size.

questions.q: Investigators derive a model to predict postoperative mortality from data on a cohort of patients undergoing surgery for hip fractures. The final model includes variables for heart function (ejection fraction), kidney function (creatinine), and age. Asthma was assessed for inclusion in the model, but did not affect the prediction. The model was found to have excellent discrimination (sensitivity = 0.91, specificity = 0.93, c-statistic = 0.88) and internal calibration. Which of the following is true?
opts: The positive predictive values can be calculated from the provided performance characteristics.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study. See the explanation under it.
The model performance indicates that it would be useful for risk stratification.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study. See the explanation under it.
Asthma is a confounder and thus excluded from the final model.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study. See the explanation under it.
Age confounds the other model variables and could be removed from the prediction model.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study. See the explanation under it.
Age, creatinine, and ejection fraction are risk factors for postoperative mortality in this study.

Correct. Prediction models are derived from multivariable methods to identify a set of variables that each improves the prediction of the outcome of interest. The final model shows how risk factors can be used together to improve prediction. In single risk factor studies, the model is used to control for other confounders to determine the independent effect of the variable of primary interest. Even models that perform well in the derivation population need to be validated independently in different populations. In addition, studies assessing the impact of the model on clinical outcomes also are an important part of model validation.

questions.q: Which of the following best characterizes the application of Bayesian reasoning to a clinical trial?
opts: Prior belief in the comparative effectiveness of treatment is guided by equipoise.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study. See the explanation under it.
The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study.
Correct. Bayesian reasoning is about how new information affects prior belief and has nothing to do with inferential statistics or the ethical rationale for randomized trials.
Bayesian inference is an alternative way of calculating a P value.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study. See the explanation under it.
Bayesian reasoning is based, like inferential statistics, on the null hypothesis.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study. See the explanation under it.
Bayesian reasoning depends on a well-defined hypothesis before the study is begun.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The results of each new study change belief in treatment effect from what it was before the study. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: In a randomized trial of intensive glucose lowering in type 2 diabetes, death rate was higher in the intensively treated patients: hazard ratio 1.22 (95% confidence interval 1.01–1.46). Which of the following is not true about this study?
opts: The results are consistent with almost no effect.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval. See the explanation under it.
The best estimate of treatment effect is a hazard ratio of 1.22.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval. See the explanation under it.
If a P value were calculated, the results would be statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval. See the explanation under it.
A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval.

Correct. The results are consistent with a 1% up to a 46% higher death rate, with the best estimate being 22% higher, and excludes a hazard ratio of 1.0 (no effect), so it is “statistically significant.” Confidence intervals provide more information than a P value for the same data because they include the point estimate and range of values that is likely to include the true effect.
The results are consistent with 46% higher death rates in the intensively treated patients.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A P value would provide as much information as the confidence interval. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: One of your patients read that cell phones cause brain cancer, and she wants to know your opinion. You discover that the incidence of malignant brain tumors is increasing in the United States. Results of several observational studies of cell phone use and brain cancer have not agreed with each other. A randomized controlled trial might resolve the question. What is the main reason why a randomized controlled trial (RCT) would be unlikely for this question?
opts: It would cost too much.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: People would not agree to be randomized to cell phone use. See the explanation under it.
People would not agree to be randomized to cell phone use.
Correct. It would be unethical to randomly allocate a potentially harmful activity, and people would probably not accept long-term restrictions on their use of cell phones.
It would take too long.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: People would not agree to be randomized to cell phone use. See the explanation under it.
Even if done well, a randomized trial could not answer the question.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: People would not agree to be randomized to cell phone use. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following would be least consistent with the belief that cell phone use is a cause of brain cancer?
opts: A dose–response relationship
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers. See the explanation under it.
A large effect size (such as relative risk)
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers. See the explanation under it.
Separate analyses of patients with right- and left-sided tumors in relation to the side they usually listened to their cell phone
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers. See the explanation under it.
A biologic explanation for why cell phones might cause cancer
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers. See the explanation under it.
Cell phone use is associated with many different kinds of cancers

Correct. All responses, which reflect the Bradford Hill criteria, would be useful in deciding whether cell phones cause brain cancer, but E, a lack of specificity, is weaker than the rest. (Consider how many diseases cigarette smoking causes.)

questions.q: Which of the following is the most accurate description of a causal relationship?
opts: Tuberculosis has a single cause, the tubercle bacillus.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Coronary heart disease has multiple interacting causes. See the explanation under it.
Most genetic diseases are caused only by an abnormal gene.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Coronary heart disease has multiple interacting causes. See the explanation under it.
Coronary heart disease has multiple interacting causes.

Correct. Figure 12.1 shows how several risk factors act together to cause coronary heart disease. Nearly all diseases are caused by the joint effect of genes and environment. Figure 12.3 shows a huge decline in tuberculosis rate before effective treatment was established in the 1950s.
Effective treatment has been the main cause of decline in tuberculosis rates.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Coronary heart disease has multiple interacting causes. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is not one of the Bradford Hill criteria for causation?
opts: Dose–response
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Statistical significance. See the explanation under it.
Statistical significance

Correct. In the absence of bias, statistical significance establishes that an association is unlikely to be by chance whereas the Bradford Hill criteria go beyond that to establish whether an association is cause and effect.
Reversibility
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Statistical significance. See the explanation under it.
Biologic plausibility
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Statistical significance. See the explanation under it.
Analogy
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Statistical significance. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: A study of the colorectal cancer screening comparing fecal occult blood testing to no screening finds that screening costs $20,000 per year of life saved. This study is an example of which of the following?
opts: Cost–benefit analysis
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cost-effectiveness analysis. See the explanation under it.
Decision analysis
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cost-effectiveness analysis. See the explanation under it.
Cost-effectiveness analysis
Correct. Cost-effectiveness analyses describe financial costs per clinical effects, such as year of life saved, as in this example, for alternative tests and treatments.
A clinical decision rule
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Cost-effectiveness analysis. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about aggregate risk studies?
opts: Aggregate risk studies are not susceptible to confounding.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: An ecological fallacy might affect their validity. See the explanation under it.
Multiple time-series studies cannot provide strong evidence of cause and effect.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: An ecological fallacy might affect their validity. See the explanation under it.
Studies relating average exposure to average risk can provide a strong test of a causal hypothesis.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: An ecological fallacy might affect their validity. See the explanation under it.
An ecological fallacy might affect their validity.

Correct. When exposure and disease are measured in groups, not individuals, it is possible that the individuals who got the disease were not the ones who were exposed and that people who were exposed were not the ones who got the disease, a problem called the “ecological fallacy.”

questions.q: Which of the following would weaken belief that the “MRSA package” (see graph) caused the observed decline in MRSA infections in VA acute care hospitals?
opts: Better antibiotics became available around the time of the program.

Correct. In a time-series study, a change in the rate of disease after an intervention might be caused by other changes in local conditions at about the same time. This possibility needs to be ruled out before one can have confidence that the study exposure caused the outcome.
Hand washing, a part of the MRSA package, increased after the program was introduced.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Better antibiotics became available around the time of the program. See the explanation under it.
The rate of MRSA infections was stable for the years before the program was introduced.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Better antibiotics became available around the time of the program. See the explanation under it.
Decline in rates began just after the program was introduced.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Better antibiotics became available around the time of the program. See the explanation under it.
questions.alt: Health-care-associated MRSA infections per 1,000 patient-days from October 2005 to June 2010, falling after the program was introduced across the VA hospitals.

questions.q: Randomized controlled trials are the strongest research designs for establishing cause and effect. Which of the following is the main limitation of trials for this purpose?
opts: Clinical trials may not be ethical or feasible for some questions.

Correct. Randomized controlled trials, if well designed and carried out, are the strongest evidence for cause and effect. But they are not possible for many suspected causes because it is not ethical to involve people in studies of harm and because they may not be willing to cooperate with such a trial.
Randomized trials cannot control for unmeasured confounders.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Clinical trials may not be ethical or feasible for some questions. See the explanation under it.
Type of study design is only a crude measure of the scientific strength.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Clinical trials may not be ethical or feasible for some questions. See the explanation under it.
Results of poorly designed and conducted trials are no better than for observational studies.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Clinical trials may not be ethical or feasible for some questions. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following provides the strongest evidence for a cause-and- effect relationship?
opts: Observational studies that have controlled for bias and minimized the role of chance.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria. See the explanation under it.
A biologic mechanism can explain the relationship.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria. See the explanation under it.
The purported cause clearly precedes the effect.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria. See the explanation under it.
There is a dose–response relationship.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria. See the explanation under it.
The evidence as a whole is consistent with the Bradford Hill criteria.
Correct. The pattern of evidence from all of the Bradford Hill criteria is more powerful than evidence for any one of them.

questions.q: You discover that case-control studies have been done to determine whether cell phone use is associated with the development of brain cancer. In one study, patients with brain cancer and matched controls without brain cancer were asked about cell phone use. The estimated relative risk for at least 100 hours of use compared to no use was 1.0 for all types of brain cancers combined (95% confidence interval 0.6–1.5). This finding is consistent with all of the following except:
opts: Use of cell phones increases the incidence of brain cancers by 50%.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The study has adequate statistical power to answer the research question. See the explanation under it.
Use of cell phones protects against brain cancers.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The study has adequate statistical power to answer the research question. See the explanation under it.
Specific types of cancers might be associated with cell phone use.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The study has adequate statistical power to answer the research question. See the explanation under it.
The study has adequate statistical power to answer the research question.

Correct. The confidence interval is so wide that it is consistent with either harm or benefit and, therefore, does not even establish whether there is an association between cell phones and brain cancer, let alone whether cell phones are a cause.

questions.q: A systematic review of observational studies of antioxidant vitamins to prevent cardiovascular disease combined the results of 12 studies to obtain a summary effect size and confidence interval. Which of the following would be the strongest rationale for combining study results?
opts: You wish to obtain a more generalizable conclusion.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size. See the explanation under it.
A statistical test shows that the studies are heterogeneous.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size. See the explanation under it.
Most of the component studies are statistically significant.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size. See the explanation under it.
The component studies have different, and to some extent complementary, biases.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size. See the explanation under it.
You can obtain a more precise estimate of effect size.

Correct. The main advantage of combining (pooling) study results in a systematic review is to have a larger sample size and as a result a more stable and precise estimate of effect size. Although it could be argued that the results are somewhat more generalizable because they come from more than one time and place, generalizability is not the main advantage.

questions.q: You are asked to critique a review of the literature on whether alcohol is a risk factor for breast cancer. The reviewer has searched MEDLINE and found several observational studies of this question but has not searched elsewhere. All of the following are limitations of this search strategy except:
opts: Studies with negative results tend to not be published.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched for both content area and methods. See the explanation under it.
MEDLINE searches typically miss some articles, even those included in the database.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched for both content area and methods. See the explanation under it.
MEDLINE does not include all of the world's journals.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched for both content area and methods. See the explanation under it.
MEDLINE can be simultaneously searched for both content area and methods.

Correct. MEDLINE can be searched using both content and methods terms, but it does not include all of the world's journals, searches miss some of the articles in MEDLINE, and they are not a remedy for publication bias since all citations in it are published. These limitations are why reviewers need to use other, complementary ways of searching for articles in addition to MEDLINE.

questions.q: A systematic review of antiplatelet drugs for cardiovascular disease prevention combined individual patients, not trials. Which of the following is an advantage of this approach?
opts: It allows for ecological comparisons.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are possible. See the explanation under it.
It is more efficient for the investigator.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are possible. See the explanation under it.
Subgroup analyses are possible.

Correct. Although individual studies usually have limited statistical power in subgroups, pooling of several studies may overcome this problem, as long as patients, not trials, are pooled. Individual comparisons can avoid the ecological fallacy that can occur with comparing group characteristics.
It is not necessary to choose between fixed and random effects models when combining data.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are possible. See the explanation under it.
Publication bias is less likely.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subgroup analyses are possible. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is not generally used to define a specific clinical question studied by randomized controlled trials?
opts: Covariates that were taken into account

Correct. B–E are elements of PICO, core components of a specific research question. Covariates are a critical aspect of the research, especially for observational studies and to identify effect modification in clinical trials, but they are about how successfully the question can be answered, not the question itself.
Interventions (e.g., exposure or experimental treatment)
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Covariates that were taken into account. See the explanation under it.
Comparison group (e.g., patients taking placebo in a randomized trial)
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Covariates that were taken into account. See the explanation under it.
Outcomes
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Covariates that were taken into account. See the explanation under it.
Patients in the trials
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Covariates that were taken into account. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes ways of measuring study quality?
opts: The validity of summary measures of study quality is well established.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A description of study quality is a useful part of systematic reviews. See the explanation under it.
A description of study quality is a useful part of systematic reviews.

Correct. Systematic reviews should include a description of the methodologic strength of the studies to help users understand how strong the conclusions are. Combining individual elements of quality into a summary measure is less well established, perhaps because it is not meaningful to give each element the same weight.
In a summary measure of quality, strengths of the study can make up for weaknesses.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A description of study quality is a useful part of systematic reviews. See the explanation under it.
Individual measures of quality such as randomization and blinding are not associated with study results.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A description of study quality is a useful part of systematic reviews. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following kinds of studies is least likely to be published?

Not the best answer. The best answer is: Small negative studies. See the explanation under it.
Large negative studies

Large positive studies
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Small negative studies. See the explanation under it.
Small negative studies

Correct. The usual situation is that small negative studies (ones that find no effect) are less likely to be published than small studies that find effects. Large studies are likely to be published no matter what they find.

questions.q: Which of the following is a comparative advantage of traditional (“narrative”) reviews over systematic reviews?
opts: Readers can confirm that evidence cited is selected without bias.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition. See the explanation under it.
Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition.

Correct. Narrative reviews can take a comprehensive approach to the set of questions clinicians must answer to manage a patient but that is at the expense of a transparent description of the scientific basis for the evidence cited.
They rely on the experience and judgment of an expert in the field.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition. See the explanation under it.
They provide a quantitative summary of effects.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition. See the explanation under it.
The scientific strength of the studies cited is explicitly evaluated.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Narrative reviews can review a broad range of questions bearing on the care of a condition. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is not always part of a typical forest plot?

Not the best answer. The best answer is: A summary or pooled effect size with confidence interval. See the explanation under it.

Point estimates of effect size for each study

Confidence intervals for each study

The size or weight contributed by each study
Not the best answer. The best answer is: A summary or pooled effect size with confidence interval. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following cannot be used for identifying severity of illness as a reason for heterogeneity in a systematic review with meta-analysis?

Correct. It is not possible to control for a covariate in a study-level meta- analysis, as one might in one of the parent studies or in a patient-level meta- analysis.
A mathematical model relating average severity of illness to outcome across the component studies

A comparison of summary effect sizes in studies stratified by mean severity of illness

Subgroup analyses of patient-level data

questions.q: Which of the following is the best justification for combining the results of five studies into a single summary effect?
opts: A statistical test does not detect heterogeneity.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar. See the explanation under it.
All studies are of high quality.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar. See the explanation under it.
The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar.

Correct. Pooling is justified if there is relatively little heterogeneity across studies, as determined by an informed review of the patient, interventions, and outcomes. A statistical rest for heterogeneity is also useful in general, but not in this case, with so few studies, because of low statistical power.
Publication bias has been ruled out by a funnel plot.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar. See the explanation under it.
The random effects model will be used to calculate the summary effect size.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The patients, interventions, and outcomes are relatively similar. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is most correct for network meta-analyses?
opts: Multiple interventions are directly compared to each other and ranked.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: They do not require similar interventions for analysis. See the explanation under it.
They require individual-level patient data for the analysis.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: They do not require similar interventions for analysis. See the explanation under it.
They require randomized controlled trials for analysis.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: They do not require similar interventions for analysis. See the explanation under it.

Correct. Network meta-analyses can use observational or randomized data to obtain both direct and indirect comparisons among interventions or tests. They can use study-level or patient-level data for analysis. The interventions can be diverse, as long as they are on similar patients and address similar outcomes.
They show the additional effects of new studies on the summary estimate.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: They do not require similar interventions for analysis. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of the random effects model over the fixed effect model?
opts: It can be used for studies with time-to-event analyses.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies. See the explanation under it.
It describes the summary effect size for a single, narrowly defined question.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies. See the explanation under it.
It is better suited for meta-analyses of diagnostic test performance.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies. See the explanation under it.
Confidence intervals tend to be narrower.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies. See the explanation under it.
It gives more realistic results when there is heterogeneity among studies.

Correct. Random effect models take heterogeneity into account, at least if it is not extreme, and, therefore, result in wider confidence intervals, which are more likely to be accurate than the narrower confidence intervals that would result from a fixed effect model.

questions.q: You are finishing residency and will begin practice. You want to establish a plan for keeping up with new developments in your field even though there are few professional colleagues in your community. All of the following might be useful, but which will be most useful to you?

Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subscribe to a service that reviews the literature in your field. See the explanation under it.
Subscribe to a service that reviews the literature in your field.
Correct. It is virtually impossible to keep up with all scientifically strong, clinically relevant new research in your field without help from a publication that does that for you.
Buy new editions of printed textbooks.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subscribe to a service that reviews the literature in your field. See the explanation under it.
Search MEDLINE at regular intervals.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subscribe to a service that reviews the literature in your field. See the explanation under it.
Keep up contacts with colleagues in your training program by e-mail and telephone.

questions.q: You can rely on the best general medical journals in your field to:
opts: Provide answers to clinical questions.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Expose you to the many dimensions of your profession. See the explanation under it.
Assure that you have kept up with the medical literature.

Guarantee that the information they contain is beyond reproach.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Expose you to the many dimensions of your profession. See the explanation under it.
Expose you to the many dimensions of your profession.

Correct. Journals are a rich source if information on the many aspects of being a physician—the history, politics, science, ideas, experiences, and more—but are not particularly good for finding answers to immediate questions or even surveillance on new developments in your field.

questions.q: Many children in your practice have attacks of otitis media. You want to base your management on the best available evidence. Which of the following is the least credible source of information on this question?
