Not the best answer. The best answer is: The most recent research article on this question. See the explanation under it.
A systematic review published in a major journal
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The most recent research article on this question. See the explanation under it.
The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The most recent research article on this question. See the explanation under it.
The most recent research article on this question

Correct. The resources listed in A–C are all excellent for looking up the answers to clinical questions, whereas a recent article, out of context with others of the same question, is of marginal value unless it happens to be much stronger than all the others that preceded it.

questions.q: A search of MEDLINE is especially useful for which of the following?
opts: Finding all of the best articles bearing on a clinical question
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Looking for reports of rare events. See the explanation under it.
An efficient strategy for finding the good articles
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Looking for reports of rare events. See the explanation under it.
Looking for reports of rare events

Correct. PubMed searches are indispensable for finding whether a rare event has been reported. They are one important part of an effort to find all published articles on a specific clinical question and are useful for researchers, but they are too inefficient for most questions at the point of care.
Keeping up with the medical literature
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Looking for reports of rare events. See the explanation under it.
Being familiar with the medical profession as a whole
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Looking for reports of rare events. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is accomplished by peer review of research manuscripts before they are published?
opts: Exclude articles by authors with a conflict of interest.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Make the published article accurate and trustworthy. See the explanation under it.
Make the published article accurate and trustworthy.
Correct. Although peer review and editing make articles better (more readable, accurate, and complete), articles are far from perfect when the process is over and they are published.
Relieve readers of the need to be skeptical about the study.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Make the published article accurate and trustworthy. See the explanation under it.
Decide for the editors about whether they should publish the manuscript.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Make the published article accurate and trustworthy. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: An author of an article showing that screening colonoscopy is more effective in preventing colorectal cancer than other forms of screening would have conflicts of interest if he or she had any of the following except:
opts: Clinical income from performing colonoscopies
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Investment in medical products in general. See the explanation under it.
Investment in a company that makes colonoscopies
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Investment in medical products in general. See the explanation under it.
Investment in medical products in general
Correct. Conflict of interest is in relation to a specific activity and does not exist in the general case of investing in medical products not specifically related to colonoscopy.
Publications of articles that have consistently advocated colonoscopy as the best screening test
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Investment in medical products in general. See the explanation under it.
Rivalry with other scholars who advocate another screening test
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Investment in medical products in general. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following is the least useful way of looking up answers to clinical questions at the point of care?
opts: Subscribing to several journals and keeping them available where you see patients

Correct. B–E are all valuable resources for looking up the answers to clinical questions at the point of care (if computers and the relevant programs are available). Medical journals have great value for other reasons, but they are not useful for this purpose.
Guidelines on http://www.guidelines.gov
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subscribing to several journals and keeping them available where you see patients. See the explanation under it.
The Cochrane Library on the Internet
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subscribing to several journals and keeping them available where you see patients. See the explanation under it.
A continually updated electronic textbook
Not the best answer. The best answer is: Subscribing to several journals and keeping them available where you see patients. See the explanation under it.

questions.q: Which of the following should be least reassuring to a patient about the quality of a web site providing information about HIV?

The site provides facts, not opinions.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The author is a well-known expert in the field. See the explanation under it.
The primary source of information is stated.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The author is a well-known expert in the field. See the explanation under it.
The date of the last revision is posted and recent.
Not the best answer. The best answer is: The author is a well-known expert in the field. See the explanation under it.
The author is a well-known expert in the field.

Correct. Patients and clinicians alike might well respect famous experts but should look for more solid footing—the organization that sponsors them, facts, and the source of those facts—when deciding whether to believe them.

questions.q: Which of the following is not part of grading clinical recommendations using the GRADE system?
opts: Deciding whether to use a diagnostic test
Correct. GRADE provides a transparent method of grading the certainty of evidence, but by necessity relies on subjective judgment in the decisions.
